content: Bedaquiline is not effective for treating viral infections, such as the common cold or influenza. How to Use: Before starting bedaquiline, and each time you receive a refill, carefully read the Medication Guide provided by your pharmacist. Take this medication orally with food as directed by your physician. Typically, it is taken once daily for the first two weeks, followed by three times a week for the next 22 weeks. The dosage is determined based on your medical condition, age, and response to treatment. Swallow the 100-milligram tablets whole, as instructed by the manufacturer. While some immediate-release tablets of other medications can be split or crushed, this is not recommended for bedaquiline. If you are using the 20-milligram tablets and have difficulty swallowing them, you may take your dose in one of two ways: 1. Add your dose (up to five tablets) to one teaspoon (5 milliliters) of water in a cup and mix thoroughly. You can either swallow the mixture immediately or add it to at least one teaspoon (5 milliliters) of a beverage or soft food and consume it right away. Suitable beverages include water, milk products, apple juice, orange juice, cranberry juice, or carbonated drinks. Soft foods such as yogurt, applesauce, mashed banana, or porridge can also be used. Ensure you take the entire dose by rinsing the cup with a beverage or soft food and swallowing it immediately. 2. Crush the tablets and mix them with soft food, such as yogurt, applesauce, mashed banana, or porridge. Mix well and consume the entire mixture immediately. To ensure the full dose is taken, add more soft food and swallow it right away. The 20-milligram tablets may also be administered through a feeding tube if necessary. For optimal effectiveness, take this antibiotic at evenly spaced intervals. If you are taking it daily, take it at the same time each day. If you are taking it three times a week, ensure doses are spaced at least 48 hours apart and taken on the same days each week (e.g., Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays) at the same time of day. Continue taking this medication, along with other tuberculosis (TB) medications, for the full prescribed duration, even if symptoms improve after a few days. Side Effects: Common side effects may include nausea, joint pain, and headache. This medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Bedaquiline may cause a rash, which is usually not serious. However, it can be difficult to distinguish between a mild rash and a rare rash that may indicate a severe reaction. Severe allergic reactions to this drug are rare. Precautions: Before taking bedaquiline, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it or have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. Bedaquiline may cause a condition that affects heart rhythm, known as QT prolongation. The risk of QT prolongation may increase if you have certain medical conditions or are taking other drugs that can cause QT prolongation. Low levels of potassium or magnesium in the blood can also increase this risk. This risk may be further elevated if you are using certain medications (e.g., diuretics or water pills) or have conditions such as severe sweating, diarrhea, or vomiting. Avoid alcohol, as it may increase the risk of liver disease. Bedaquiline may reduce the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine. During pregnancy, this medication should only be used when clearly necessary. Bedaquiline passes into breast milk and may have undesirable effects on a nursing infant. Drug Interactions: Drug interactions may alter how your medications work or increase the risk of serious side effects. Keep a list of all the products you use, including prescription and non-prescription drugs and herbal products, and share it with your doctor and pharmacist. Other medications may affect the removal of bedaquiline from your body, potentially altering its effectiveness. Overdose: If someone has overdosed and exhibits serious symptoms such as passing out or difficulty breathing, call emergency services immediately (911 in the U.S.). Otherwise, contact a poison control center right away. U.S. residents can call 1-800-222-1222. Missed Dose: If you miss a daily dose during the first two weeks of treatment, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. If you miss a dose from week three onward, take it as soon as you remember, then return to your usual three-times-a-week dosing schedule. Ensure there is at least 24 hours between doses, and do not exceed the weekly dose within a seven-day period. Storage: Store this medication in its original container at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep the drying agent (desiccant) in the bottle if you are using the 20-milligram tablets. If necessary, the 100-milligram tablets may be stored in another container for up to three months. Always tightly close the bottle when not in use. Do not flush medications down the toilet or pour them into a drain unless instructed to do so. Properly discard this product when it is expired or no longer needed. Important Notes: This information is a summary and does not contain all possible details about this product. It does not guarantee that this product is safe, effective, or appropriate for you. Always consult your healthcare professional for complete information about this product and your specific health needs. Warning: Bedaquiline may cause QT prolongation, a condition that affects heart rhythm. The risk of QT prolongation may increase if you are taking other drugs that can cause this condition. Uses: This medication is used in combination with other drugs to treat active multi-drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB) of the lungs in individuals with limited treatment options. Bedaquiline belongs to a class of drugs known as antibiotics. It treats bacterial infections only and will not work for viral infections such as the common cold or flu.
